questions.q: Which of these is NOT a function of the kidney?
questions.explain: Bile salts are made by the liver. The kidney excretes waste, regulates water, electrolytes and acid-base balance, and secretes erythropoietin, renin and calcitriol.

questions.q: What is the approximate blood flow to both kidneys per minute at rest?
questions.explain: The kidneys are about 0.5% of body weight but receive roughly a quarter of the cardiac output.

open.q: What is the approximate blood flow to both kidneys per minute at rest?

questions.q: Which hormone made by the kidney stimulates red cell production?
questions.explain: Peritubular interstitial cells release erythropoietin in response to hypoxia. Loss of it in kidney failure causes anaemia.

open.q: Which hormone made by the kidney stimulates red cell production?

questions.q: Which active form of vitamin D is made by the kidney?
questions.explain: The proximal tubule hydroxylates 25-hydroxycholecalciferol at the 1 position, giving calcitriol.

open.q: Which active form of vitamin D is made by the kidney?

questions.q: What is the functional unit of the kidney?
questions.explain: Each nephron has a renal corpuscle and a tubule, and forms urine on its own.

open.q: What is the functional unit of the kidney?

questions.q: Roughly how many nephrons are in each human kidney?
questions.explain: Each kidney has about 1 to 1.3 million nephrons. They cannot regenerate, so loss is permanent.

open.q: Roughly how many nephrons are in each human kidney?

questions.q: What does the renal corpuscle consist of?
options: Bowman's capsule and loop of Henle
questions.explain: The renal corpuscle is the filtering part of the nephron: a tuft of capillaries inside a double-walled capsule.

open.q: What does the renal corpuscle consist of?

questions.q: Which cells form the visceral layer of Bowman's capsule?
questions.explain: Podocytes wrap around the glomerular capillaries with foot processes, leaving filtration slits between them.

open.q: Which cells form the visceral layer of Bowman's capsule?

questions.q: Which nephron type has the long loop of Henle that dips deep into the medulla and is important for concentrating urine?
questions.explain: Only about 15% of nephrons are juxtamedullary, but their long loops and vasa recta create the medullary gradient.

open.q: Which nephron type has the long loop of Henle that dips deep into the medulla and is important for concentrating urine?

questions.q: The brush border is a feature of which part of the nephron?
questions.explain: Microvilli greatly increase the surface area for the large reabsorptive load of the proximal tubule.

open.q: The brush border is a feature of which part of the nephron?

questions.q: What are the three layers of the glomerular filtration membrane?
options: Continuous endothelium, basement membrane and tight junctions
Fenestrated endothelium, glomerular basement membrane and slit diaphragm
Fenestrated endothelium and Bowman's capsule only
questions.explain: The negatively charged basement membrane and slit diaphragms restrict albumin and larger proteins.

open.q: What are the three layers of the glomerular filtration membrane?
accept: fenestrated endothelium, basement membrane, slit pores

questions.q: Which cells of the juxtaglomerular apparatus secrete renin?
options: Juxtaglomerular granular cells of the afferent arteriole
questions.explain: JG cells are modified smooth muscle cells with renin granules.

open.q: Which cells of the juxtaglomerular apparatus secrete renin?

questions.q: The macula densa is part of the wall of which tubule segment?
questions.explain: Macula densa cells sense NaCl delivery to the distal tubule and signal the glomerulus.

open.q: The macula densa is part of the wall of which tubule segment?

questions.q: Name a stimulus for renin release.
options: A rise in renal arterial pressure
Increased NaCl delivery to the macula densa
A fall in renal arterial pressure
questions.explain: Renin is released by low pressure in the afferent arteriole, low NaCl at the macula densa, and sympathetic (β1) stimulation.

open.q: Name a stimulus for renin release.
open.a: A fall in renal arterial pressure (also low NaCl at the macula densa and sympathetic stimulation)

questions.q: Renin acts on which substrate?
questions.explain: Renin cleaves angiotensinogen from the liver to form angiotensin I.

open.q: Renin acts on which substrate?

questions.q: Which enzyme converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II?
questions.explain: ACE works mainly on the endothelium of lung capillaries. ACE inhibitors block this step.

open.q: Which enzyme converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II?

questions.q: Which is NOT an action of angiotensin II?
options: Stimulation of ADH release and thirst
questions.explain: Angiotensin II stimulates aldosterone secretion from the adrenal cortex.

questions.q: Name the vessels, in order, that blood passes through from the afferent arteriole onwards.
options: Efferent arteriole → glomerulus → afferent arteriole → peritubular capillaries
Interlobular artery → peritubular capillaries → glomerulus → efferent arteriole
Afferent arteriole → glomerulus → efferent arteriole → peritubular capillaries
Arcuate artery → efferent arteriole → glomerulus → afferent arteriole
questions.explain: Blood passes through two capillary beds in series, the glomerular and the peritubular.

open.q: Name the vessels, in order, that blood passes through from the afferent arteriole onwards.
accept: afferent arteriole, glomerulus, efferent arteriole, peritubular capillaries

questions.q: Between which two kinds of vessels does the glomerular capillary bed lie?
questions.explain: This arrangement lets the kidney keep a high glomerular pressure (about 60 mmHg).

open.q: Between which two kinds of vessels does the glomerular capillary bed lie?

questions.q: Which vessels supply the renal medulla and help preserve its concentration gradient?
questions.explain: The vasa recta act as countercurrent exchangers.

open.q: Which vessels supply the renal medulla and help preserve its concentration gradient?

questions.q: What fraction of the plasma entering the glomeruli is filtered (filtration fraction)?
questions.explain: GFR 125 ml/min divided by renal plasma flow about 625 ml/min gives about 0.2.

open.q: What fraction of the plasma entering the glomeruli is filtered (filtration fraction)?

questions.q: Over roughly what range of mean arterial pressure does renal autoregulation keep blood flow constant?
questions.explain: Within this range, renal blood flow and GFR barely change. Below it, filtration falls.

open.q: Over roughly what range of mean arterial pressure does renal autoregulation keep blood flow constant?

questions.q: Which two mechanisms are mainly responsible for renal autoregulation?
questions.explain: Stretch of the afferent arteriole causes it to constrict (myogenic). Macula densa signals adjust the afferent arteriole (feedback).

open.q: Which two mechanisms are mainly responsible for renal autoregulation?

questions.q: Which substance's clearance is used to measure renal plasma flow?
questions.explain: PAH is almost completely removed from plasma in one pass, so its clearance approximates renal plasma flow.

open.q: Which substance's clearance is used to measure renal plasma flow?

questions.q: The kidneys lie in the retroperitoneum at approximately which vertebral levels?
questions.explain: The kidneys extend from about the 12th thoracic to the 3rd lumbar vertebra, partly protected by the lower ribs.

open.q: Between which vertebral levels do the kidneys lie?
accept: Thoracolumbar region down to the third lumbar vertebra

questions.q: Why does the right kidney usually lie slightly lower than the left?
options: Presence of the spleen above it
Presence of the liver above it
Pull of the right adrenal gland
questions.explain: The large right lobe of the liver pushes the right kidney down by about 1 to 2 cm.

open.q: Why does the right kidney usually lie slightly lower than the left?
accept: Right lobe of the liver pushes it down

questions.q: The renal hilum lies at approximately which vertebral level?
questions.explain: The hilum lies near L1, close to the transpyloric plane, and transmits the renal vessels and pelvis.

open.q: At approximately which vertebral level does the renal hilum lie?

questions.q: From front to back, which is the order of structures at the renal hilum?
options: Renal pelvis, renal artery, renal vein
Renal artery, renal vein, renal pelvis
Renal vein, renal pelvis, renal artery
Renal vein, renal artery, renal pelvis
questions.explain: The renal vein is most anterior, then the renal artery, then the renal pelvis posteriorly. The mnemonic is vein, artery, pelvis.

open.q: From front to back, in what order do the renal vein, renal artery and renal pelvis lie at the hilum?

questions.q: Which layer of fat lies directly outside the fibrous capsule of the kidney and inside the renal fascia?
questions.explain: From inside out the kidney is covered by the fibrous capsule, perirenal fat, renal fascia (Gerota), then pararenal fat.

open.q: Which layer of fat lies directly outside the fibrous capsule of the kidney and inside the renal fascia?

questions.q: What are the extensions of renal cortex that pass between the renal pyramids called?
questions.explain: Renal columns of Bertin are cortical tissue dipping between pyramids and carry interlobar vessels. Medullary rays are striations of the medulla extending into the cortex.

open.q: What name is given to the extensions of renal cortex that pass between the renal pyramids?

questions.q: Urine leaving the tip of a renal pyramid drains first into which structure?
questions.explain: The papilla opens into a minor calyx. Minor calyces unite into major calyces, which join to form the renal pelvis.

open.q: Into which structure does urine drain first after leaving the tip of a renal pyramid?

questions.q: Approximately how many nephrons does each human kidney contain?
questions.explain: Each kidney has about one million nephrons. Nephrons cannot regenerate, so numbers fall with age and disease.

open.q: Approximately how many nephrons does each human kidney contain?

questions.q: What proportion of nephrons are cortical nephrons?
questions.explain: About 85% of nephrons are cortical with short loops of Henle. The remaining 15% are juxtamedullary.

open.q: What proportion of nephrons are cortical nephrons?

questions.q: Which type of nephron has long loops of Henle reaching deep into the medulla and is most important for concentrating urine?
questions.explain: Juxtamedullary nephrons have glomeruli near the corticomedullary junction, long loops of Henle and vasa recta, which build the medullary concentration gradient.

open.q: Which type of nephron has long loops of Henle reaching deep into the medulla and is most important for concentrating urine?

questions.q: Which protein is the main component of the filtration slit diaphragm between podocyte foot processes?
questions.explain: Nephrin forms the slit diaphragm and mutation of its gene causes congenital nephrotic syndrome. Collagen IV and laminin are in the basement membrane.

open.q: Which protein is the main component of the slit diaphragm between podocyte foot processes?

questions.q: What is the correct order of the glomerular filtration barrier layers, from capillary lumen to Bowman's space?
options: Fenestrated endothelium, basement membrane, podocyte slit diaphragms
Podocyte slit diaphragms, basement membrane, fenestrated endothelium
Basement membrane, fenestrated endothelium, podocyte slit diaphragms
Fenestrated endothelium, podocyte slit diaphragms, basement membrane
questions.explain: Filtrate crosses the fenestrated endothelium, then the glomerular basement membrane, then the slit diaphragms between podocyte foot processes.

open.q: From capillary lumen to Bowman's space, what are the three layers of the glomerular filtration barrier in order?
accept: Endothelium, glomerular basement membrane, podocyte foot processes
Endothelium then GBM then slit diaphragm

questions.q: Which cells lie between glomerular capillary loops, support them, and can contract to alter the filtration surface area?
questions.explain: Intraglomerular mesangial cells are contractile and phagocytic and secrete matrix. They differ from the extraglomerular mesangial cells of the juxtaglomerular apparatus.

open.q: Which cells lie between glomerular capillary loops, support them, and can contract to alter the filtration surface area?

questions.q: Which nephron segment has a prominent brush border of microvilli?
questions.explain: The brush border greatly increases the surface area of the proximal tubule, which reabsorbs most of the filtrate.

open.q: Which nephron segment has a prominent brush border of microvilli?

questions.q: The macula densa is a specialised region of which tubular segment?
options: Thick ascending limb at the start of the distal tubule
questions.explain: The macula densa is a plaque of tall, closely packed cells at the start of the distal tubule where it touches its own glomerulus's vascular pole.

open.q: The macula densa is a specialised region of the wall of which tubular segment?

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a component of the juxtaglomerular apparatus?
questions.explain: The juxtaglomerular apparatus comprises the macula densa, granular JG cells and extraglomerular mesangial (lacis) cells. Podocytes belong to the filtration barrier.

questions.q: What does the macula densa directly sense?
options: Sodium chloride delivery in tubular fluid
questions.explain: Macula densa cells detect NaCl delivery in the tubular fluid, partly through the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter, and signal to the arterioles of the same nephron.

open.q: What does the macula densa directly monitor in the tubular fluid?
accept: Sodium chloride concentration in tubular fluid

questions.q: In tubuloglomerular feedback, a rise in NaCl delivery to the macula densa causes which response?
questions.explain: Raised NaCl delivery triggers release of vasoconstrictor signals such as adenosine, which narrow the afferent arteriole and lower GFR, restoring delivery to normal.

open.q: In tubuloglomerular feedback, what happens to the afferent arteriole when NaCl delivery to the macula densa rises?

questions.q: At rest, renal blood flow is approximately:
questions.explain: The kidneys receive about 1200 mL/min, roughly 20 to 25% of cardiac output, although they are under 1% of body weight.

open.q: Approximately what is the resting renal blood flow in mL/min?

questions.q: Which arteries run between the renal pyramids, within the renal columns?
questions.explain: Segmental arteries give interlobar arteries in the renal columns. These give arcuate arteries at the corticomedullary junction, then interlobular arteries and afferent arterioles.

open.q: Which arteries run between the renal pyramids, within the renal columns?
accept: Interlobar branches of the renal artery

questions.q: Blood in the kidney passes through two capillary beds in series. Which vessel lies between them?
questions.explain: The efferent arteriole carries blood from the glomerular capillaries to the peritubular capillaries or vasa recta. This arrangement allows glomerular pressure to be regulated independently of peritubular pressure.

open.q: Blood in the kidney passes through two capillary beds in series. Which vessel lies between them?

questions.q: From which vessels do the vasa recta arise?
questions.explain: Long efferent arterioles of juxtamedullary nephrons give straight vessels that run alongside the loops of Henle and maintain the medullary gradient.

open.q: From which vessels do the vasa recta arise?

questions.q: Approximately what proportion of renal blood flow goes to the cortex?
questions.explain: About 90% of renal blood flow supplies the cortex. The low medullary flow helps preserve the concentration gradient but makes the medulla vulnerable to hypoxia.

open.q: Approximately what proportion of renal blood flow goes to the renal cortex?

questions.q: Over which approximate range of mean arterial pressure do the kidneys autoregulate renal blood flow and GFR?
questions.explain: Between about 80 and 180 mmHg, myogenic and tubuloglomerular mechanisms keep flow and GFR nearly constant. Below this range, GFR falls steeply.

open.q: Over which approximate range of mean arterial pressure do the kidneys autoregulate renal blood flow and GFR?

questions.q: What underlies the myogenic mechanism of renal autoregulation?
options: Release of ADH from the posterior pituitary
Stretch-induced contraction of afferent arteriolar smooth muscle
Sympathetic discharge to the efferent arteriole
Angiotensin II release by the macula densa
questions.explain: A rise in arterial pressure stretches the afferent arteriole, which responds by contracting and so limits the rise in glomerular pressure.

open.q: What underlies the myogenic mechanism of renal autoregulation?
accept: Arteriolar smooth muscle contracts when stretched
Stretch of afferent arteriole causes constriction
Pressure-induced vasoconstriction of the afferent arteriole

questions.q: Glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure is approximately:
questions.explain: Glomerular capillary pressure is about 60 mmHg, much higher than in most capillaries, because the afferent arteriole is wide and the efferent arteriole is narrow.

open.q: Approximately what is the hydrostatic pressure in the glomerular capillaries?

questions.q: A dehydrated patient takes ibuprofen and develops acute kidney injury. Which mechanism best explains the fall in GFR?
options: Efferent arteriolar dilation by angiotensin II
Increased renin release causing afferent dilation
Afferent constriction after loss of prostaglandin-mediated dilation
questions.explain: In volume depletion, vasodilator prostaglandins keep the afferent arteriole open against vasoconstrictors. NSAIDs block them, so afferent constriction lowers glomerular pressure and GFR.

open.q: A dehydrated patient takes ibuprofen and develops acute kidney injury. By what mechanism does the drug lower GFR?
accept: Inhibition of prostaglandins causing afferent constriction
Afferent arteriole vasoconstriction from loss of prostaglandins

questions.q: A patient with bilateral renal artery stenosis is started on an ACE inhibitor and creatinine rises sharply. Why?
options: Efferent dilation after loss of angiotensin-II tone, lowering glomerular pressure
questions.explain: With low perfusion pressure, angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole and so maintains glomerular pressure. Blocking it dilates the efferent arteriole and GFR falls.

open.q: A patient with bilateral renal artery stenosis is started on an ACE inhibitor and creatinine rises sharply. Why?
accept: Efferent arteriole dilation lowering glomerular capillary pressure
Fall in efferent tone and GFR

questions.q: A child with oedema has heavy albuminuria. Renal biopsy shows diffuse podocyte foot-process effacement. Which component of the filtration barrier is most directly disrupted?
options: The podocyte slit-diaphragm and foot-process architecture
The mesangial matrix between capillary loops
The parietal epithelium of Bowman's capsule
questions.explain: Minimal change disease is characterised by diffuse podocyte foot-process effacement and disruption of the slit-diaphragm filtration interface. This increases permeability to plasma proteins, especially albumin. It should not be explained simply as loss of negative charge selectivity; the precise molecular basis of protein leak is more complex.

open.q: Which part of the glomerular filtration barrier is disrupted by podocyte foot-process effacement in minimal change disease?
accept: podocyte foot processes and slit diaphragm

questions.sub: Renal blood flow and GFR autoregulation
questions.q: A healthy adult has a brief rise in arterial pressure from 100 to 150 mmHg. Despite the pressure increase, renal blood flow and glomerular filtration rate change only modestly. Which intrinsic response most directly contributes to this stability?
options: Constriction of the afferent arteriole in response to stretch of its smooth muscle
Dilation of the efferent arteriole caused by increased macula densa sodium delivery
Increased renin release causing systemic vasoconstriction
Relaxation of the afferent arteriole in response to increased transmural pressure
questions.explain: The myogenic response is an intrinsic renal autoregulatory mechanism: increased pressure stretches afferent arteriolar smooth muscle, which contracts and limits the rise in renal blood flow and glomerular capillary pressure. Tubuloglomerular feedback provides a complementary mechanism: increased NaCl delivery to the macula densa promotes afferent arteriolar constriction and suppresses renin release. Autoregulation helps stabilise renal blood flow and GFR over the usual autoregulatory pressure range; it does not make them completely pressure-independent.

questions.q: A dehydrated patient has a rise in plasma protein concentration. Which direct change in glomerular Starling forces tends to reduce GFR?
options: Reduced hydrostatic pressure in Bowman's space
Reduced oncotic pressure in glomerular capillaries
questions.explain: Higher plasma protein concentration raises glomerular capillary oncotic pressure, opposing movement of fluid into Bowman's space and lowering net filtration pressure.

open.q: How does increased plasma protein concentration affect glomerular filtration?
accept: raises glomerular oncotic pressure and reduces GFR

questions.q: A healthy adult receives a drug that selectively dilates the afferent arteriole without changing efferent arteriolar tone. What is the immediate expected effect?
options: Reduced renal blood flow and reduced GFR
Increased renal blood flow and increased GFR
Increased renal blood flow but reduced GFR
No change in glomerular capillary pressure
questions.explain: Afferent dilation lowers resistance before the glomerulus, increasing renal blood flow and glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure; GFR therefore rises.

open.q: What happens to renal blood flow and GFR when the afferent arteriole dilates?
accept: increases renal blood flow and GFR

questions.q: During severe haemorrhage, marked sympathetic activation helps preserve arterial pressure. What is its direct effect on renal arterioles at high sympathetic activity?
options: Afferent arteriolar constriction, reducing renal blood flow and GFR
Afferent arteriolar dilation, increasing renal blood flow
questions.explain: Strong renal sympathetic activity constricts renal arterioles, particularly the afferent arteriole, reducing renal perfusion and filtration while supporting systemic blood pressure.

open.q: What does strong renal sympathetic activation do to afferent arteriolar tone and GFR?
accept: constricts afferent arteriole and reduces GFR

questions.q: A glomerulus has a capillary hydrostatic pressure of 55 mmHg, Bowman's space hydrostatic pressure of 15 mmHg, and glomerular capillary oncotic pressure of 25 mmHg. If Bowman's space oncotic pressure is negligible, what is the net filtration pressure?
questions.explain: Net filtration pressure is 55 − 15 − 25 = 15 mmHg when Bowman's space oncotic pressure is negligible.

open.q: How is net filtration pressure calculated from glomerular hydrostatic and oncotic pressures?
accept: glomerular hydrostatic pressure minus Bowman's space hydrostatic and glomerular oncotic pressures

questions.q: A patient with chronic glomerulosclerosis has fewer functioning filtration capillary loops, while the measured Starling pressures remain similar. Which variable in the GFR equation is most directly reduced?
questions.explain: Loss of functioning filtration surface area lowers the filtration coefficient (Kf), reducing GFR even if the pressure gradients are unchanged.

open.q: Which GFR variable falls when functioning glomerular filtration surface area is lost?
